function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It covers everything you asked for:

1. **Clone the repo**  
2. **Analyse** the repo and generate the required files  
3. **Add / Commit / Push** the changes

> ⚠️ **Important** – I can’t actually run the commands for you, but the commands below will do exactly what you need when executed in a shell that has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl` and `yq` (or any YAML editor) installed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH access, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Generate Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

> The repo is a simple Node.js app (look for `package.json` and `app.js`).  
> We’ll use the official `node:18-alpine` image (the latest LTS at the time of writing).

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# 1️⃣ Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# 2️⃣ Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# 3️⃣ Copy package files first (to leverage Docker cache)
COPY package*.json ./

# 4️⃣ Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 5️⃣ Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# 6️⃣ Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 7️⃣ Default command
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and production‑ready.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposing port `3000` matches the default port used by most Node.js starter apps.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

> We’ll create a **Deployment** and a **Service** that expose the app inside the cluster.

Create a directory `k8s` (or put the file directly in the repo root) and add `nodejs-welcome.yaml`:

```yaml
# k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Notes**  
> * The image tag `latest` is a placeholder – you’ll replace it with the actual image you push (see the GitHub Actions section).  
> * `ClusterIP` is the default; change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

> Build the Docker image and push it to Docker Hub (or any registry) whenever code is pushed to `main`.

Create the directory `.github/workflows` and add `build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to set up:**
> 1. Create a Docker Hub account (or use another registry).  
> 2. In the repo’s **Settings → Secrets → Actions**, add:
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password)

---

## 3️⃣ Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# 3. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml

# 4. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 5. Push to remote
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to Docker Hub.  
> You can verify the build status on the **Actions** tab of the repo.

---

## 4️⃣ Verify Everything Works

1. **Build locally** (optional):

   ```bash
   docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:local .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:local
   ```

   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to see the app.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (if you have `kubectl` configured):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml
   ```

   Check pods:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
   ```

   Expose the service externally (if needed) or use `kubectl port-forward` to test.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes Docker image |

Feel free to tweak the image tag, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
